PraisonAI codeMode sandbox-escape RCE: node process spawning OS shell / recon binaries AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a Node.js process running PraisonAI (praisonai-ts codeMode tool) spawning a shell, recon, or transfer binary. The codeMode sandbox is supposed to run JS in-process only; any child_process/execSync-spawned OS command from that node process is the direct manifestation of the Function-constructor blocklist bypass (GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84). The PoC literally ran `id` via cp.execSync. Rationale: Anchors on the article's exact component (praisonai / codeMode) as the node parent plus a shell/recon child, because the sandbox is designed to run JS in-process only — a child OS process from it is the bypass executing. The PoC's `id` recon is included. Cross-checked GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp and CVE-2026-40158 which confirm child_process recovery via the Function constructor. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-40158/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.004 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A PraisonAI deployment whose node command line legitimately invokes the python_tools subprocess sandbox (spawns python3)
  • Build/CI tooling running under the same node process tree (npm scripts, node-gyp, webpack) shelling out
  • Process managers like pm2/nodemon restarting and spawning sh
  • Container entrypoint scripts where node is PID 1 and forks a shell for health checks
  • Developer running node REPL with child_process during local testing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("npm","node-gyp","yarn","webpack","install","healthcheck") and not (FileName =~ "python3" and ProcessCommandLine has "_execute_code_sandboxed")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the child ChildCmd and parent ParentCmd — confirm the parent node is actually running praisonai (check folder/cmdline) and the child is not a build/health-check script. Note the OS command run (id/whoami/curl indicate hands-on-keyboard). 2) Contain: isolate the host/container, kill the node process tree, and rotate any API keys/tokens/secrets present in that process's environment (env-var exfil is the stated impact). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/aid for outbound egress from node (UC3), for written persistence files, and confirm the praisonai version — upgrade to >=1.7.2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node","node.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai"
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","node-gyp","yarn","webpack","install"))
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python3")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType == "ProcessCreated"
| where ActingProcessName has "node"
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai" or ActingProcessName has "praisonai"
| where not(ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("npm","node-gyp","yarn","webpack"))
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/bin/sh","/bin/bash","/bin/dash","/usr/bin/zsh","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","/usr/bin/id","whoami","uname","hostname","curl","wget","ncat")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI codeMode component present on host (code-mode.ts/js under praisonai) AIReconnaissance High
Asset-discovery hunt for the vulnerable file path named in the advisory — src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts (and its compiled code-mode.js) under any praisonai directory. Surfaces every host/container carrying the exploitable codeMode tool so they can be confirmed against the patched 1.7.2 release. Rationale: Uses the advisory's exact vulnerable file path (src/praisonai-ts/src/tools/builtins/code-mode.ts) plus the compiled .js form to enumerate exposure. High confidence the file maps to the affected component; version confirmation (vs patched 1.7.2 from GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp) separates vulnerable from fixed. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84
ATT&CKT1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts running the PATCHED praisonai >=1.7.2 which still ships a code-mode file (fixed, not vulnerable) — verify package.json/version
  • Source-code mirrors, package caches, or git clones of praisonai-ts that are not actually executed
  • Security researchers' local checkout of the advisory PoC
  • Backup/restore images surfacing historical node_modules
  • Container image-build layers scanned by the EDR during CI
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, resolve the installed praisonai version (read package.json near the FolderPath or query the package manager) and whether codeMode is enabled for any agent. 2) Contain: on confirmed vulnerable (1.4.0–1.7.1) production hosts, disable the codeMode tool and/or upgrade to >=1.7.2; restrict the node process's egress and secrets exposure in the interim. 3) Hunt: correlate the host against UC1 (node spawning shells) and UC3 (node novel egress) to determine whether the vuln was merely present or actually exploited.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "praisonai"
| where FileName in~ ("code-mode.ts","code-mode.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), arg_max(Timestamp, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName) by DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has "praisonai"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("code-mode.ts","code-mode.js")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName
| order by LastSeen desc

PraisonAI node process novel outbound egress (post-escape secret/API-key exfiltration or C2) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts a node process running PraisonAI making outbound connections to destinations outside the expected set of LLM/API/registry endpoints. After the codeMode escape, the stated impact is exfiltrating environment variables (API keys, tokens) and installing backdoors — both produce egress from the node process to attacker infrastructure not seen in a normal agent's API traffic. Rationale: Anchors on the praisonai node process (so it's article-specific, not generic node egress) and the advisory's named impact of env-var/API-key exfiltration and backdoor install. Excludes the normal LLM/API/registry endpoints an agent legitimately calls so residual hits are candidate exfil/C2. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p69m-4f92-2v84
ATT&CKT1041 T1552.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The agent legitimately calling a self-hosted or less-common LLM/inference endpoint not in the allowlist (e.g. private Ollama host, Together/Groq/Bedrock endpoints)
  • Tool/plugin functionality that fetches external web content as part of normal agent tasks
  • Telemetry/APM SDKs bundled in the node app beaconing to vendor SaaS
  • Package/dependency fetches via a private registry mirror
  • CDN/object-storage pulls for model or asset downloads
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".bedrock.amazonaws.com" and RemoteUrl !has_any ("together.ai","groq.com","datadoghq.com","sentry.io")
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the destination(s) — resolve WHOIS/reputation and whether they are known LLM/SaaS infra; check timing against any UC1 shell-spawn hit on the same host. 2) Contain: if the destination is unrecognized, block it at egress, isolate the host/container, and immediately rotate all secrets in the node process environment (the named impact is API-key/token theft). 3) Hunt: inspect the node process tree for child shells (UC1) and for newly written startup/backdoor files; expand the allowlist for confirmed-benign endpoints to tune the hunt.

PraisonAI codeMode escape: Node.js process spawning OS shell for recon/secret access AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the post-escape behaviour of the PraisonAI codeMode sandbox break: a node host process spawning an OS shell (sh/bash/cmd/powershell) whose command line performs environment/credential/file recon. After `({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()` recovers `process.mainModule.require`, attacker code calls child_process to run commands the sandbox was meant to block. A node process that is only supposed to run 'sandboxed' JS should never shell out to read /etc/passwd, .env or printenv. Rationale: Uses the article's stated post-escape impact (child_process subprocess execution, reading env vars and host files) anchored on a node parent process — the one binary that hosts codeMode. Recon-token filter on the child command line keeps it from firing on every legitimate node->shell call. Cross-checked GHSA and the GitLab advisory mirror (fixed 1.7.2) plus public vm-escape write-ups showing the canonical execSync('cat /etc/passwd') payload. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://thegoodhacker.com/posts/the-unsecure-node-vm-module/ • https://github.com/vercel/workflow/issues/1026
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Node app legitimately shelling out via child_process to git/imagemagick/ffmpeg during normal operation
  • npm/yarn lifecycle scripts (postinstall) invoking bash that runs uname/base64 during builds
  • node-gyp compiling native modules and reading system files
  • CI/CD runners using a node orchestrator to launch bash provisioning steps
  • Monitoring/backup agents written in Node that call whoami/hostname for inventory
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","npm ","yarn ","prebuild","node_modules/.bin","/usr/lib/node_modules") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","prebuild-install"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full child command line and the node parent's command line/working dir; confirm whether this host runs a praisonai/codeMode agent endpoint and whether the recon target (.env, /etc/passwd, printenv) is legitimate for that service. 2) Contain: if unexplained, isolate the host, rotate any API keys/service tokens reachable from the node process environment, and quarantine the node service pending review. 3) Hunt: search the same host for sibling node->shell executions, outbound connections from node to new domains/IPs (exfil), and any process command line containing 'constructor.constructor' or 'process.mainModule.require'; pin the praisonai package version and upgrade to >=1.7.2.

PraisonAI codeMode Function-constructor prototype-chain escape payload signature AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact JavaScript escape primitive used to break out of codeMode's fake sandbox: the prototype-chain recovery of the real Function constructor (`({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()`) combined with `process.mainModule.require`. When this payload transits a command line, application/syslog stream, or captured request body it is a near-zero-FP indicator of an attempted codeMode (or any Node vm/new Function) sandbox escape. Rationale: Targets the literal escape gadget the advisory documents (`({}).constructor.constructor('return process')()` -> `process.mainModule.require`), which the blocklist never covers; the two-token pairing (constructor.constructor + mainModule/return process) makes legitimate occurrence vanishingly rare. Datadog uses case-insensitive full-text phrase search so no casing enumeration is needed. Cross-checked against public Node vm/new Function escape research confirming the same gadget. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/praisonai/GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp/ • https://thegoodhacker.com/posts/the-unsecure-node-vm-module/ • https://architecture.pub/articles/410978448.html
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1211
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SAST/dependency scanners or pentest tooling replaying the advisory PoC against your own apps
  • The PraisonAI regression/PoV test (poc/pov_poc.js) executing in CI or a developer sandbox
  • Security researchers or red team validating GHSA-vmmj-pfw7-fjwp in a lab
  • Application logs verbosely echoing a blocked/sanitised request body that contained the payload
  • Developer documentation or a blog/notebook about Node sandbox escapes being opened/built on the host
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pov_poc.js","semgrep","trivy","grype","npm test","jest","mocha") or FolderPath has_any ("/poc/","\\test\\","/test/","node_modules"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full payload and its source (which process/log stream, which app endpoint, which user/IP submitted it) and determine whether it reached a live codeMode/vm sink or was logged after being blocked. 2) Contain: block the source IP/user at the agent/tool API, take the affected node service out of rotation, and rotate any secrets present in that process environment (API keys, service tokens). 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (node spawning shells) on the same host and time window, review outbound connections from the node process for exfil, confirm praisonai is patched to >=1.7.2, and audit other tool endpoints that funnel user/LLM content into new Function or vm.

INC Ransomware BYOVD vulnerable driver drop (filwfp.sys / filnk.sys / fildds.sys) AIInstallation High
Hunts the file write or load of the three named vulnerable kernel drivers INC ransomware affiliates use to blind EDR/AV before encryption. These filenames are not legitimate Windows or vendor drivers, so any appearance is high-fidelity; Sophos observed all three loaded onto one network within seven minutes. Rationale: Uses the three exact BYOVD driver filenames from the article, independently confirmed by Sophos X-Ops (three loads in 7 minutes on one network). No legitimate driver carries these names, so a bare file-create match is high fidelity. INC Rust encryptor launched with --esxi hypervisor argument AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of a process invoked with INC ransomware's documented '--esxi' command-line flag, which triggers the Rust encryptor to shut down running virtual machines before encrypting ESXi datastores. Targets Linux/ESXi hosts where Defender for Endpoint or auditd telemetry is available. Rationale: The '--esxi' operator flag that drives the encryptor to power off VMs is stated verbatim in the article and corroborated by Acronis/CybersecurityNews reporting on the Rust Linux/ESXi variant. It is an unusual token rarely seen in benign command lines. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/inc-ransomware-uses-rust-based-windows/amp/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/inc-ransomware-thrives-by-mastering-the-basics
ATT&CKT1486 T1529
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin VM-migration or DR scripts that pass an --esxi parameter to an internal tool
  • Backup/replication jobs invoking ESXi automation with a similar flag
  • Security testing of ESXi-targeting tooling in a lab cluster
Suppression filter
| where not(FolderPath has_any ("/usr/lib/vmware", "/opt/vmware")) and FileName !in~ ("vim-cmd", "esxcli", "vmware-vim-cmd")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the binary is unsigned/unknown and not a sanctioned VMware utility; check the host for simultaneous mass VM power-off (vim-cmd / esxcli vm process kill). 2) Contain: power-isolate the ESXi host from management/storage networks and snapshot datastores if not yet encrypted. 3) Hunt: review the host for the BYOVD driver drops, rclone exfil, and lateral RDP/PsExec inbound from the same operator account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "--esxi" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "--esxi"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated asc

INC Ransomware Rclone cloud exfiltration of staged archives AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts INC's data-theft step: rclone (or a renamed rclone identified by its characteristic flags) copying/syncing data to an external cloud remote after the operator stages it as password-protected archives. Catches both the named binary and renamed copies via flag fingerprinting. Rationale: Rclone is the exfiltration tool named in the article; the renamed-binary fallback fingerprints rclone's distinctive --config/--transfers/--multi-thread-streams flags so a rename to evade the binary-name match still fires. Pairs with the article's password-protected-archive staging (T1560.001). Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/inc-ransomware-thrives-by-mastering-the-basics
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT/backup teams using rclone for legitimate cloud backup or migration
  • DevOps syncing artifacts to S3/B2/GDrive via rclone in CI
  • Personal-use rclone on a developer workstation copying to a cloud remote
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe", "backup-agent.exe") and AccountName !startswith "svc-backup"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the rclone command line for the remote target and source path; cloud destinations (mega/b2/onedrive) sourcing from file shares or backup volumes are high risk. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at egress, suspend the executing account, and preserve the rclone config (often holds the attacker's remote creds). 3) Hunt: look for 7-Zip/WinRAR/rar processes creating password-protected (-p/-hp) archives on the same host just before, and correlate with BYOVD driver drops signalling imminent encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "rclone.exe"
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "--config"
       and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--transfers", "--multi-thread-streams", "--no-check-certificate", "--ignore-existing")
       and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("copy", "sync", "move"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rclone.exe"
   or (CommandLine has "--config"
       and (CommandLine has "--transfers" or CommandLine has "--multi-thread-streams" or CommandLine has "--no-check-certificate")
       and (CommandLine has "copy" or CommandLine has "sync" or CommandLine has "move"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated asc

INC Veeam backup credential dumping (salted DPAPI SQL secret access) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts INC's updated credential dumper reading Veeam Backup & Replication's stored SQL credentials (SqlLogin / SqlSecuredPassword DPAPI blobs) or the VeeamBackup Credentials table from a non-Veeam process on a backup server. Targets the credential-access step that lets INC neutralize recovery before encryption. Rationale: Anchors on Veeam's real credential-store internals — the SqlLogin/SqlSecuredPassword DPAPI registry values under 'Veeam Backup and Replication' and the VeeamBackup [Credentials] table — which the article's salted-DPAPI Veeam dumper must touch; the non-Veeam-parent filter keeps it focused on the attacker tool, not the product itself. Cross-checked against: • https://www.acronis.com/en/tru/posts/from-emerging-threat-to-top-tier-ransomware-as-a-service-the-evolution-of-inc-ransomware/ • https://securitybrief.com.au/story/inc-ransomware-surges-as-australia-stays-in-sights
ATT&CKT1003 T1555 T1552.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam admins running official credential-migration or upgrade scripts
  • Backup-monitoring tooling querying the VeeamBackup config DB
  • DBA running ad-hoc SELECTs against the VeeamBackup database during troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("veeamadmin", "svc-veeam") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sqlservr.exe", "postgres.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the executing binary/account is not a sanctioned Veeam component or admin; review whether it ran on a designated backup server. 2) Contain: rotate all credentials stored in Veeam (service, repository, vCenter/ESXi, cloud) and isolate the backup server, since dumped creds enable backup deletion and lateral movement. 3) Hunt: trace the operator account to inbound RDP/RMM sessions, look for backup-job or repository deletion, and the BYOVD driver drops that precede INC encryption.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "Veeam Backup and Replication" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SqlSecuredPassword", "SqlLogin"))
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "VeeamBackup" and ProcessCommandLine has "Credentials")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe", "Veeam.Backup.Service.exe", "Veeam.Backup.PowerShell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp asc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (TargetProcessCommandLine has "Veeam Backup and Replication" and TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("SqlSecuredPassword", "SqlLogin"))
     or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "VeeamBackup" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "Credentials")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("Veeam.Backup.Manager.exe", "Veeam.Backup.Service.exe", "Veeam.Backup.PowerShell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName,
          TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated asc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

status: experimental
description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-3519", "CVE-2025-5777", "CVE-2023-48788", "CVE-2024-57727")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2023-3519", "CVE-2025-5777", "CVE-2023-48788", "CVE-2024-57727")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count

    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

    category: process_creation

            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'

Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:

    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:

            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /api/mcp/connect MCP endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PraisonAI UI (aiui) server spawns shell/LOLBin child via unauth MCP connect RCE · [LLM] PraisonAI MCP RCE proof-of-concept marker file written to /tmp · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w: PraisonAI: Missing Authentication for Cri
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
PraisonAI UI (aiui) server spawns shell/LOLBin child via unauth MCP connect RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation execution step of GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w: the PraisonAI UI host app (launched via `aiui run` / `praisonai ui` / `praisonai claw`) starting an attacker-chosen local process through the MCP stdio transport. Legitimate MCP stdio servers are npx/uvx/node/python runtimes; a raw shell, touch, curl, wget or nc child of the aiui server is the RCE signature. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact server-launch strings (`aiui run`, `praisonai ui`, `praisonai claw` from ui.py/claw.py) as the parent and a raw shell/LOLBin child — no legitimate MCP stdio server is a bare shell. Datadog left empty because linux.auditd EXECVE in this tenant exposes no parent-process field to anchor the aiui pivot. Falcon limited to ParentBaseFileName since FDR ProcessRollup2 carries no parent command line. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/mcp-bridge/GHSA-wvr4-3wq4-gpc5/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://github.com/MervinPraison/PraisonAI/security/advisories/GHSA-9qhq-v63v-fv3j
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1059
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately-configured MCP server whose stdio command is a shell wrapper script (e.g. a `bash -c` launcher around a real MCP binary)
  • Admin/SRE debugging the aiui service from the same process tree (interactive shell under the service)
  • An MCP server config that uses curl/wget to fetch from a package registry on startup
  • Health-check or readiness probe scripts shelling out under the service account
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","pypi.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd — confirm the child is a real shell/exfil tool, not an MCP runtime, and check whether the aiui service is internet-exposed (bound 0.0.0.0). 2) Contain: kill the child PID, isolate/cordon the host, and immediately set `AUTH_ENFORCE=true` (or take the UI offline) so /api/mcp/connect is no longer unauthenticated; rotate any secrets readable by the UI service user. 3) Hunt: review proxy/web logs for prior POSTs to /api/mcp/connect, enumerate sibling children of the aiui process, and check for follow-on persistence (cron, systemd units, SSH keys) written by the same account.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aiui run","praisonai ui","praisonai claw","create_host_app","build_host_app") or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "aiui"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","ksh","fish","busybox","touch","curl","wget","nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64","whoami","id","uname","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| where not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("registry.npmjs.org","pypi.org","ghcr.io","objects.githubusercontent.com"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("aiui run","praisonai ui","praisonai claw","create_host_app","build_host_app")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/ksh","/fish","busybox","touch","curl","wget","/nc","ncat","socat","chmod","base64","whoami","/id","uname","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentCmd = ActingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = TargetProcessName, ChildCmd = TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI /api/mcp/connect MCP endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the vulnerable PraisonAIUI route `POST /api/mcp/connect` (and `/api/mcp/servers`) exposed by the UI host app on 0.0.0.0 without auth. Surfaces exploitation attempts at the wire level before code executes, complementing the host-side process detection. Rationale: Uses the article's exact route strings `/api/mcp/connect` and `/api/mcp/servers` (registered at praisonaiui/server.py:2769-2770) plus the POST method from the documented PoC request. Defender/Falcon/Datadog/CloudWatch empty because the request body and URI live only in proxy/web-access logs, not in EDR or AWS CloudTrail telemetry in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p75f-6fp4-p57w • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/npm/mcp-bridge/GHSA-wvr4-3wq4-gpc5/

Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate operator adding an MCP server through the PraisonAI UI, which issues the same POST /api/mcp/connect from the browser
  • Internal vulnerability scanner or ASM probe hitting the endpoint
  • CI/CD smoke test that exercises the MCP connect route
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor configured to POST to the API path
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the SourceIP — is it external/untrusted or an internal admin workstation? Correlate the timestamp against UC1 process-spawn alerts on the destination host. 2) Contain: if the source is untrusted, block it at the WAF/proxy and restrict the aiui listener to localhost or behind authenticated reverse proxy (set AUTH_ENFORCE=true). 3) Hunt: pull all requests from that SourceIP, look for repeated POSTs (PoC retries until the process wins scheduling) and any subsequent host-side child-process execution.

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Vulnerable PraisonAI package inventory (CVE-2026-40151, >= 4.2.1 <= 4.6.57) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PraisonAI AgentOS process bound to 0.0.0.0:8000 / external inbound connections
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] PraisonAI AgentOS unauthenticated POST /api/chat remote agent invocation
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
PraisonAI AgentOS unauthenticated POST /api/chat remote agent invocation AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP requests to the AgentOS FastAPI routes POST /api/chat and GET /api/agents that return 200 with no Authorization header — the exact incomplete-fix surface in CVE-2026-40151. A no-auth 200 on these paths means an external client successfully enumerated or drove the deployed agent (triggering its tools, memory, and cost-bearing model calls). Rationale: Uses the article's exact incomplete-fix routes (POST /api/chat, GET /api/agents) and the documented behaviour that no-auth requests return 200 (vs 401 on the hardened sibling control). HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization empty + 200 is the clean true positive for unauthenticated invocation; corroborated by the GHSA, the CVE-2026-40151 record, and public reports of rapid endpoint scanning. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Kubernetes liveness/readiness probes GETting /api/agents (UA kube-probe)
  • Cloud load-balancer health checks (ELB-HealthChecker) hitting the route
  • An upstream API gateway that terminated auth at the edge, so the backend log shows no Authorization header
  • CI/CD smoke tests invoking the deployed agent post-deploy
  • Internal developers calling the API directly on a trusted network where auth was intentionally disabled
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1","::1") and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "kube-probe" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "ELB-HealthChecker" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "GoogleHC"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all 200 responses to /api/chat and /api/agents grouped by source IP; confirm whether the caller is external (non-RFC1918, not a known LB/proxy) and whether the Authorization header was absent. Check the AgentOS process owner and what tools/memory the agent wraps. 2) Contain: place the AgentOS listener behind an authenticating reverse proxy or rebind to 127.0.0.1, or block port 8000 at the perimeter immediately; rotate any API keys/secrets the agent had access to. 3) Hunt: review request bodies for /api/chat to identify what messages were sent (data exfiltration, tool abuse), pivot on the source IP across other internet-facing assets, and check for the GET /api/agents enumeration that typically precedes invocation.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/chat" or Url has "/api/agents"
| where HttpMethod in~ ("POST","GET")
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no bearer token presented
| where HttpStatusCode == 200                      // vulnerable AgentOS returns 200, a patched/proxied one returns 401
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, UserAgent=HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

PraisonAI AgentOS process bound to 0.0.0.0:8000 / external inbound connections AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the misconfiguration root cause: a PraisonAI/uvicorn process launched with the default host=0.0.0.0 port=8000 and/or accepting inbound connections from public IPs on 8000. This is the network-exposure precondition that makes the unauthenticated AgentOS routes reachable. Rationale: Anchors on the article's literal config defaults (host="0.0.0.0", port=8000) and the praisonai/AgentOS/AgentApp module names, plus public inbound on 8000. This catches the exposed-listener root cause regardless of whether an exploit request has landed yet — the 0.0.0.0 default is called out as the root cause in the advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-40151-cwe-200-exposure-of-sensitive-infor-41548a8f
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional production deployment with AgentOS on 0.0.0.0 but fronted by an authenticating reverse proxy (the advisory's recommended pattern)
  • Containers binding 0.0.0.0 inside an isolated pod network with no real internet exposure
  • Dev/test instances deliberately reachable on a trusted LAN
  • Public inbound connections that are actually from a known ingress controller / WAF source IP, not real external clients
Suppression filter
| where RemoteIPs !has "10." and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "127.0.0.1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit, determine whether the host is genuinely internet-facing (DeviceInfo IsInternetFacing / public IP) and whether an authenticating proxy sits in front of port 8000. 2) Contain: if exposed without auth, rebind AgentOS to 127.0.0.1 or place it behind a bearer-auth proxy and firewall port 8000; treat as exploitable per CVE-2026-40151 since v4.5.128–v4.6.57 and main are all vulnerable. 3) Hunt: cross-reference with web-log UC1 to see if any unauthenticated /api/chat or /api/agents 200s already occurred against this listener, and inventory other hosts running the same praisonai version.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8000
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","python3","python.exe","python3.exe","uvicorn","gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","agentos","AgentApp","AgentOS")
| summarize ConnCount=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), RemoteIPs=make_set(RemoteIP, 100) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalPort
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","agentos","AgentApp","AgentOS")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "0.0.0.0" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "8000"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Surfaces hosts with the praisonai / praisonaiagents package installed in the confirmed-vulnerable range (incl. the supposedly-patched v4.5.128 and latest v4.6.57). Used to scope exposure for the unauthenticated AgentOS incomplete-fix advisory. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id (CVE-2026-40151) and the advisory's confirmed-affected range (>= 4.2.1, <= 4.6.57 — including the falsely-patched 4.5.128 and latest 4.6.57). This is posture scoping: it tells the SOC which assets need the network-exposure and web-log detections applied. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-892r-p3jq-jp24 • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-892r-p3jq-jp24
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM inventory lag listing a version that was already upgraded
  • praisonai installed as a transitive dependency but AgentOS never actually deployed/served
  • Developer workstations with the package present but no network-reachable listener
  • Version strings with pre-release/dev suffixes that the regex range check mislabels — verify manually
Response runbook
1) Triage: list all hosts running praisonai/praisonaiagents and join against internet-facing status; prioritize any in the 4.2.1–4.6.57 range that also appear in the UC2 exposed-listener results. 2) Contain: since no fixed release exists yet (main still reproduces), apply compensating controls — bind to 127.0.0.1 or front with an authenticating proxy, and firewall port 8000 — rather than relying on a version bump. 3) Hunt: feed the asset list into UC1/UC2 to detect actual unauthenticated invocation, and monitor the advisory for a real fixed version to drive remediation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has "praisonai" or SoftwareName has "praisonaiagents"
| extend Vuln = iff(SoftwareVersion matches regex @"^4\.([2-5]\.|6\.([0-9]|[0-5][0-9])$)", "in-vulnerable-range(>=4.2.1,<=4.6.57)", "verify-version")
| project DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, Vuln, EndOfSupportStatus
| sort by DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-40151" or (SoftwareName has "praisonai")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| sort by DeviceName asc
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-40151")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-40151")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Unauthenticated PraisonAI AgentTeam.launch agent invocation via /agents endpoints AIExploitation Medium
Hunts external HTTP requests that hit PraisonAI's unauthenticated AgentTeam.launch()/Agents.launch() routes: GET /{path}/list (agent enumeration), POST /{path} (sequential team invocation) and POST /{path}/{agent_id} (single-agent invocation), defaulting to /agents. Because the launch path registers no auth middleware, every 200 response is by definition unauthenticated agent execution (GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp, sibling of CVE-2026-44338 / CVE-2026-40151). Rationale: Anchored on the article's concrete route shapes (GET /{path}/list, POST /{path}, POST /{path}/{agent_id}; default path /agents from the PoC) plus the fact that no Authorization parsing exists in the launch path, so any 200 from a public source IP is unauthenticated agent execution. Corroborated by sibling advisories and observed in-the-wild scanning of /agents and /chat. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://gbhackers.com/praisonai-vulnerability-actively-exploited/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/praisonai/CVE-2026-39889/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal application/front-end calling its own PraisonAI /agents API from a corporate egress IP that resolves as public
  • Authorized API consumers or partner integrations invoking the agent team intentionally
  • Security scanners / ASM tooling (e.g. internal pentest, Nuclei templates) probing /agents/list
  • Uptime monitors polling the documented /health and adjacent routes
  • DAST pipelines in CI hitting the staging endpoint
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has_any ("PraisonAI-internal", "uptime-monitor")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the full request set for the offending CIp — confirm whether /agents/list (enumeration) preceded a POST /agents or POST /agents/{id} (invocation), inspect User-Agent and request bodies for prompt-injection or data-exfil markers, and verify the source IP is not a sanctioned consumer. 2) Contain: Put the PraisonAI launch endpoint behind auth or network ACLs immediately (the launch path ships no token check); block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy and, if internet-exposed, take the service off 0.0.0.0. 3) Hunt: Review all historical hits on the route shapes, pivot on the host running the server for outbound connections or tool/agent actions triggered by the injected prompts, and confirm whether the deployment is on a patched/hardened build vs. current main.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ScStatus == 200
| where (CsMethod == "GET" and tolower(CsUriStem) endswith "/agents/list")
     or (CsMethod == "POST" and tolower(CsUriStem) matches regex @"/agents(/[^/]+)?$")
| where not(ipv4_is_private(CIp))
| summarize Requests = count(), Methods = make_set(CsMethod), Paths = make_set(CsUriStem), UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 5), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by CIp, CsHost
| order by Requests desc
title: Unauthenticated PraisonAI AgentTeam Agent Invocation Endpoint Access
id: b7e4d2a1-9c3f-4e88-a1d2-6f0b5c7e9a14
status: experimental
description: Detects access to PraisonAI AgentTeam.launch()/Agents.launch() unauthenticated routes (agent listing and agent invocation), which register no auth middleware and execute agent.chat() on any caller.
references:
    - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp
    - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj
author: SOC Detection Engineering

detection:

        cs-method: 'GET'

    selection_invoke:

        c-uri|re: '/agents(/[^/]+)?$'
    condition: selection_list or selection_invoke
falsepositives:
    - Authorized internal users of a deliberately exposed PraisonAI deployment
level: medium

Internet-facing Python host running PraisonAI Agents.launch bound to 0.0.0.0 AIDelivery Low
Hunts hosts where a Python/uvicorn process running the PraisonAI agent server accepts inbound connections from public source IPs — the exposure precondition for GHSA-x8cv-xmq7-p8xp, where Agents.launch()/AgentTeam.launch() default-binds to 0.0.0.0 and documentation shows host="0.0.0.0". Surfaces the externally reachable, unauthenticated agent-execution surface before/while it is probed. Rationale: Uses the article's specific exposure facts: launch() default bind host 0.0.0.0 and documented host="0.0.0.0" for remote access, hosted by a Python/uvicorn process, accepting public inbound. Process-name + public-inbound + praisonai cmdline/path keeps it scoped to the vulnerable surface rather than generic Python listeners. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentionally exposed, but properly proxied, PraisonAI deployment fronted by an auth gateway
  • Dev/test Python services (Flask/uvicorn) unrelated to PraisonAI that match on python.exe
  • Internal load-balancer or health-check traffic that egresses and returns as a public IP
  • Container hosts where many Python microservices accept inbound on a shared node
  • Data-science/Jupyter or API servers legitimately bound to 0.0.0.0 behind a firewall
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","AgentTeam")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the listening Python process is actually PraisonAI (inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine/FolderPath and the listening LocalPort) and determine whether the public inbound sources are sanctioned consumers or opportunistic scanners. 2) Contain: If it is an unauthenticated PraisonAI launch surface, rebind to 127.0.0.1 or place it behind an authenticating reverse proxy / network ACL, and restrict the security group/firewall to known clients. 3) Hunt: Correlate with web/proxy logs (UC1) for hits on /agents/list and POST /agents from the same source IPs, check the host for prompt-injection-driven tool actions or outbound connections, and inventory other hosts running the same vulnerable build.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","python3.exe","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("praisonai","AgentTeam",".launch","Agents") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "praisonai"
| summarize Connections = count(), DistinctSources = dcount(RemoteIP), Ports = make_set(LocalPort), SampleCmd = any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Connections desc

Vulnerable PraisonAI recipe-serve module (fail-open auth middleware) present on host AIExploitation Medium
Hunts for the exact vulnerable praisonai/recipe/serve.py (v4.6.48, sha256 491bf8f2...) whose APIKeyAuthMiddleware/JWTAuthMiddleware silently disable themselves when no secret is configured. Surfaces hosts running the at-risk component so they can be patched or have a secret enforced before the recipe-execution surface is reached unauthenticated. Rationale: Pivots on the article's exact file artifact: sha256 491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23 and path praisonai/recipe/serve.py. Hash match (Defender/Sentinel EDR) confirms the vulnerable 4.6.48 build; path match (Sysmon/FDR, which don't hash on write) is the fallback. Cross-checked against the sibling fail-open advisory CVE-2026-44338 confirming the same package's auth-disabled-by-default class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://docs.praison.ai/docs/deploy/deploy
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Intentional dev/test sandbox running praisonai where api_key/PRAISONAI_API_KEY is correctly set (vulnerable code present but not exploitable)
  • CI/build pipeline checking out or installing the praisonai package as an artifact
  • Internal red-team / security-research host that installed praisonai deliberately
  • A patched fork where serve.py was edited but the file path is unchanged (hash differs — path-only match)

// Prioritise exploitable hosts: join to internet-facing inventory
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | where IsInternetFacing == true | distinct DeviceId) on DeviceId
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is actually serving recipes (look for a running 'praisonai ... recipe serve' process / listening port) and whether it is internet-facing (DeviceInfo.IsInternetFacing). A non-running package copy is low priority. 2) CONTAIN: On any internet-facing or shared host, enforce a secret immediately — set api_key:/jwt_secret: in the recipe YAML or export PRAISONAI_API_KEY/PRAISONAI_JWT_SECRET, and restart so the middleware fails closed; restrict the listener to localhost/VPN. 3) HUNT: Pivot to UC2 (unauthenticated /runs access) and UC3 (recipe-serve spawning shells) on the same DeviceId to determine whether the fail-open window was already abused.

Unauthenticated POST to PraisonAI recipe-serve /runs execution endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Detects requests reaching the praisonai recipe-serve execution path (/runs) with no authenticated user, the exact surface left open by the fail-open middleware. Catches an attacker triggering arbitrary recipe executions without an X-API-Key / Bearer token, including the rapid post-disclosure scanning PraisonAI endpoints have seen. Rationale: Pivots on the article's concrete execution path /runs (used in the PoC Request) plus POST method and the absence of an authenticated user (CsUsername empty/'-') — the direct fingerprint of a request the silently-disabled middleware forwarded. Defender side surfaces public inbound connections to the 'recipe serve' process when web-server logs aren't in XDR. Datadog/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty: FDR/Sysmon network events lack the request-path and auth-user context, and no web-access source is in scope. Corroborated by Sysdig/CSO reporting of sub-4h scanning of PraisonAI endpoints. Cross-checked against: • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4171215/praisonai-vulnerability-gets-scanned-within-4-hours-of-disclosure.html • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation • https://docs.praison.ai/docs/deploy/deploy
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal load-balancer / health probes or uptime monitors hitting the service (note /health is always allowed by design — exclude it)
  • Legitimate clients where the front-end does not populate CsUsername even though an API key is validated downstream in the app
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tooling run by your own security team probing /runs
  • Authenticated internal automation calling /runs over a trusted network segment
Suppression filter
| where not(CIp startswith "10." or CIp startswith "192.168." or CIp startswith "172.16.")  // drop internal probes/monitors; keep external callers
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Check ScStatus on the /runs hits — 2xx means the recipe actually executed unauthenticated; pull the source IP, geo, and UserAgent and confirm whether the host's recipe YAML / env actually sets a secret (if not, every hit is a real bypass). 2) CONTAIN: Block the offending source IPs at the edge, take the recipe-serve listener off the public interface, and enforce api_key:/jwt_secret: so the middleware fails closed; rotate any secrets/data the recipes had access to. 3) HUNT: Correlate the same DeviceName/time window with UC3 (recipe-serve process spawning shells) and review recipe inputs/outputs for attacker-controlled prompts or exfil of operator data.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "recipe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "serve")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Ports=make_set(LocalPort)
          by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Connections desc
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem =~ "/runs"
| where CsMethod == "POST"
| where isempty(CsUsername) or CsUsername == "-"   // no authenticated principal == fail-open path reached
| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Statuses=make_set(ScStatus)
          by CIp, CsHost, CsUriStem, CsMethod, UserAgent
| order by Requests desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/runs*" OR Web.uri_path="/runs") Web.http_method=POST by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.status Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where user="-" OR user="" OR isnull(user) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/runs*" OR Web.uri_path="/runs") Web.http_method=POST by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.status Web.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where user="-" OR user="" OR isnull(user) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - count
PraisonAI recipe-serve agent process spawning command/script interpreter (post-bypass RCE) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the python/uvicorn process running 'praisonai recipe serve' spawning a shell or scripting interpreter — the code-execution outcome when an attacker reaches a tool-wired recipe through the fail-open auth surface. This is the RCE path the advisory calls out (recipes wired to code execution / file-system / browser automation). Rationale: Pivots on the article's specific parent context (python running 'recipe serve'/'praisonai') spawning interpreters, the documented RCE path where recipes are wired to code execution. Parent cmdline pins the praisonai context on Defender/Sentinel/Sysmon/Datadog; Falcon's ProcessRollup2 schema lacks ParentCommandLine, so it is intentionally broad (python->shell) and meant to be scoped by the host found in UC1. CloudTrail empty (endpoint detection). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6rmh-7xcm-cpxj • https://webflow.sysdig.com/blog/cve-2026-44338-praisonai-authentication-bypass-in-under-4-hours-and-the-growing-trend-of-rapid-exploitation
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate code-execution recipes (a built-in feature) where the agent intentionally shells out to run generated code
  • Browser-automation recipes spawning chromium/node (excluded from the interpreter list, but adjacent activity)
  • Operator running praisonai interactively in a dev environment and triggering shell tools
  • Package/venv setup steps under the same python process invoking sh/cmd at startup
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("whoami","curl","wget","Invoke-WebRequest","base64","/tmp/","-enc ","nc ","bash -i")  // keep only child commands with recon/download/encoding intent; drop benign recipe code-exec
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — generated code that matches the operator's expected recipe is benign; recon/download/encoded commands (whoami, curl, base64, /tmp writes) on an internet-facing recipe-serve host is a confirmed RCE. Confirm whether the host enforces an auth secret. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the recipe-serve process, take the listener off the public interface, and rotate any credentials/keys reachable from the recipe's tool environment. 3) HUNT: From the same DeviceId pull subsequent persistence (UC autostart writes), outbound C2 (DeviceNetworkEvents to public IPs from the python parent), and correlate back to the UC2 /runs source IP to scope the intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","python3.exe","python3","python","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "recipe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "serve")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","bash","sh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","python3","pythonw.exe","uvicorn.exe","python")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has "praisonai"
    or (ParentProcessCommandLine has "recipe" and ParentProcessCommandLine has "serve")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash","sh","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or SHA1 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or MD5 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or SHA1 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23") or MD5 in~ ("491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["491bf8f29e399418260810ba4bf0f6802c6e4aa675628e2be68a9726c15d9b23"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
